title: Here's how engineers plan to save the satellite sent to save NASA's Swift mission
gist: Katalyst Space Technologies' Link satellite — flying NASA's first commercial servicing contract, a $30 million job to grab and boost the $500 million Swift observatory — spun out of control a week after a nominal launch, losing two of three reaction wheels to a thermal spike caused by its own ungraceful fault-protection power cycle. Katalyst has halved the spin using gimbaled xenon electric thrusters and, with NASA, is remapping control algorithms to fly three-axis control on one wheel, still targeting a Swift rendezvous around end of August.

themes.theme: NASA's first commercial satellite servicing contract

insights.claim: Katalyst Space Technologies, a satellite servicing startup, won a $30 million NASA contract to fly its Link spacecraft to the $500 million Swift gamma-ray observatory, grab onto it and boost its orbit before atmospheric drag destroys it — the first time NASA has contracted a commercial company to service one of its own satellites.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: This contract is the reference price and reference precedent for the in-orbit servicing market; its outcome will shape whether NASA and commercial operators buy servicing as a routine line item.
insights.locator: The Link satellite is built, owned, and operated by Katalyst

insights.claim: NASA gave Katalyst less than a year to assemble the entire Swift rescue mission, and the refrigerator-size Link satellite launched July 3 and flew mostly to plan until the anomaly.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: A sub-12-month build-to-launch cycle is the schedule benchmark now set for responsive servicing missions — and a candidate contributor to the anomaly if margins were traded for speed.
insights.locator: The space agency gave Katalyst less than a year

insights.claim: The rescue has a hard orbital deadline: in a few months Swift will be too low for Katalyst to complete the capture and boost at all.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: The recovery is not just an engineering problem but a stopwatch problem — every week of despin burns irrecoverable mission margin.
insights.quote: The clock is ticking. In a few months, Swift will be too low for Katalyst to complete the rescue.

insights.claim: One week into its pursuit, the Link satellite began rotating on multiple axes more than 200 miles above Earth, which prevented a reliable ground communications link and complicated efforts to arrest the spin; two of its three reaction wheels stopped working and some cold gas thrusters developed a problem.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Loss of pointing plus loss of comms is the compounding failure mode that turns recoverable anomalies into lost spacecraft — watch whether autonomy can close that loop without ground contact.
insights.locator: One week ago, more than 200 miles above the Earth

insights.claim: The spacecraft's own fault-protection logic caused the hardware damage: after more than 24 hours without ground contact it automatically power-cycled itself as designed, but the shutdown pulled the plug on everything, producing a thermal spike that over-temperatured the electronics controlling the reaction wheels and left them inoperable.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Safe-mode design is a real reliability risk, not just a backstop — the recovery mechanism itself broke the pointing hardware, a failure pattern worth auditing across smallsat fleets.
insights.quote: Basically, there was a big thermal spike that came about as a result of this that over-temperatured the upstream electronic circuits that control the reaction wheels, which ultimately led them to being inoperable
insights.locator: This was built-in fault protection logic saying

insights.claim: Engineers still do not know what triggered the initial loss of control on the Link spacecraft — candidates include an internal problem or a collision with space junk — and two onboard cameras will search for signs of damage only after the spacecraft is stabilized.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: If debris impact is confirmed, it becomes a live datapoint for orbital-debris risk pricing in LEO servicing missions and insurance.
insights.locator: Engineers aren’t sure yet what caused the emergency

insights.claim: The cold gas thruster fault on Link appears to be a separate issue from the reaction wheel damage, but the team lacks the data to make a final determination and cannot yet separate causes from consequences.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Multiple simultaneous faults with unclear ordering usually mean the root cause investigation runs long — treat any early all-clear as provisional.
insights.quote: These things all happened at once, so it’s hard to delineate between what contributed to creating the situation and what was the consequence of the situation
insights.locator: The problem with the spacecraft’s cold gas thrusters

insights.claim: Katalyst's mission control team near Denver lost contact with Link for more than 24 hours after the spin began, with only sporadic radio contact available during the emergency.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Ground-segment resilience — not propulsion — was the binding constraint during the first day of the anomaly, an argument for higher-bandwidth or relay comms on servicing vehicles.
insights.locator: Whatever the cause, Katalyst’s mission control team lost contact

insights.claim: Katalyst is despinning Link using its three xenon-fueled electric thrusters, which are primarily designed for orbit-raising but can vector thrust through a two-axis gimbal and therefore double as attitude control.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Gimbaled electric propulsion functioning as a backup attitude-control path is a design redundancy worth pricing into servicing spacecraft architectures.
insights.quote: We’ve been able to use the thrusters to point in the opposite direction of the rotation rate and affect the attitude control that way, which has been highly effective

insights.claim: The despin has cut Link's rotation rate roughly in half, from about 9 degrees per second to approximately 4 degrees per second as of Friday, with further reduction needed to restore high-bandwidth communications.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: A measurable, monotonic despin rate is the single best public indicator of whether this recovery succeeds before the Swift orbital deadline.
insights.locator: This has worked well so far

insights.claim: Low-thrust electric propulsion makes the recovery slow by construction — it is efficient but takes time to generate enough impulse to regain full pointing control.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: The physics of the backup control path directly consumes the mission's limited schedule margin — efficiency and responsiveness trade off against each other here.
insights.locator: Link’s electric propulsion system is efficient but low in thrust

insights.claim: Rather than trying first to revive the two dead reaction wheels, Katalyst's priority is uplinking a new control algorithm that manages orientation using the one remaining reaction wheel combined with thrusters, with the guidance, navigation and control team remapping control algorithms jointly with NASA.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: Software-defined attitude control is what makes this recoverable at all — reprogrammability is the real resilience asset on modern servicing spacecraft.
insights.locator: Katalyst may eventually be able to recover the satellite’s two inoperable reaction wheels

insights.claim: Link's other critical systems stayed healthy through the anomaly, including its power supply, its three xenon-fueled electric thrusters, and the rendezvous and robotics hardware needed to capture Swift.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: The mission-critical capture payload is intact, so the mission's value is preserved if and only if attitude control is restored in time.
insights.locator: The good news was the spacecraft’s other systems remained healthy

insights.claim: Katalyst CEO Ghonhee Lee says the company still aims to move Link toward Swift around the end of August, and believes three-axis control is achievable with the remaining reaction wheel, remaining thrusters and electric propulsion.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: End of August is the checkpoint date for judging whether commercial servicing survives its first NASA test — slippage past it likely kills the capture.
insights.quote: It’s not the original mode that we expected to control the spacecraft with, but it seems like we will have sufficient stability and controllability of the spacecraft
insights.locator: Nevertheless, Lee said Katalyst still aims to move Link

insights.claim: Katalyst has not made a formal assessment but believes an attempted capture of Swift is still viable, with a close-approach inspection within a few dozen meters expected before any grapple.
insights.speaker: Stephen Clark
insights.so_what: The inspection-then-capture sequencing means there will be an observable intermediate milestone before the binary capture outcome.
insights.quote: we believe that a capture of Swift, an attempted capture of Swift, is very much in the cards
insights.locator: We believe that we’ll be able to go and do things like the inspection of Swift
